description: Olympic and twice world champion champion Lara Gut-Behrami of Switzerland will not return to alpine skiing from a severe knee injury and has ended her career. Gut-Behrami, 35, told broadcasters RSI on Wednesday evening she had "the honour to experience a long career, to express my wishes and dreams through my skiing and to experience this journey alongside extraordinary people.
fullText:
Olympic and twice world champion champion Lara Gut-Behrami of Switzerland will not return to alpine skiing from a severe knee injury and has ended her career.

Gut-Behrami, 35, told broadcasters RSI on Wednesday evening she had "the honour to experience a long career, to express my wishes and dreams through my skiing and to experience this journey alongside extraordinary people."

Gut-Behrami wanted to ski a final season in 2025-26 with the Milan/Cortina Olympics but suffered a ruptured cruciate and medial collateral ligament as well as a torn meniscus in a training accident in November 2025.

The injury sidelined her for the season and she left it open at the time whether she would add a final campaign in 2026-27.

"Despite 20 years of elite sport, crashes and injuries I have had no recurring pain and don't want to have it. For that reason as well I have the feeling that the right moment has come - the moment when I no longer have to insist, at all costs, on reaching and exceeding my limits," she said.

Gut-Behrami made her World Cup debut in 2007 and won 48 races. She won the overall World Cup twice, in 2016 and 2024, and seven discipline titles, six in super-g and one in giant slalom.

She won the super-g and giant slalom at the 2021 world championships and Olympic super-g gold a year later. In all, she has 12 medals from worlds and Olympics.

title: WTC Points Table: How Pakistan's win over West Indies changed the standings
description: Australia remain at the top of the World Test Championship standings. They have won seven of their eight matches, lost one, collected 84 points and have the best Points Percentage (PCT) of 87.50. Pakistan climbed to eighth after their win over the West Indies. They have won two and lost four of their six matches.
fullText:
Pakistan climbed one place in the World Test Championship (WTC) 2025-27 points table after beating the West Indies by eight wickets in the second Test in Trinidad. The win helped Pakistan level the two-match series 1-1 and move above the West Indies in the standings.

Earlier, Pakistan had slipped to the bottom of the table after losing the opening Test. They now have two wins from six matches and a points percentage (PCT) of 22.22.

Pakistan also ended their eight-match away losing streak in Test cricket with the victory.

Chasing a target of 77, Pakistan reached 77/2 shortly after lunch on Day 4. Abdullah Shafique, who scored a century in the first innings, remained unbeaten on 24 along with captain Babar Azam, who also finished on 24 not out.

Babar sealed the win by hitting back-to-back sixes off left-arm spinner Jomel Warrican.

West Indies had won the first Test by 90 runs in Tarouba, but Pakistan bounced back strongly in the second match. Spinners Sajid Khan and Ali Usman made the most of the conditions at Queen's Park Oval as Pakistan remained unbeaten in a Test series against the West Indies since 2000.

1. Australia (1st): Australia remain at the top of the World Test Championship standings. They have won seven of their eight matches, lost one, collected 84 points and have the best Points Percentage (PCT) of 87.50.

2. South Africa (2nd): South Africa are second with three wins and one defeat in four matches. They have 36 points and a PCT of 75.00.

3. New Zealand (3rd): New Zealand are third after winning four of their six Tests. They have one loss and one draw, with 52 points and a PCT of 72.22.

4. Bangladesh (4th): Bangladesh occupy fourth place. They have won two matches, lost one and drawn one from four Tests. They have 28 points and a PCT of 58.33.

5. India (5th): India are fifth in the standings. The Shubman Gill-led side have played nine matches, winning four, losing four and drawing one. India have 52 points and a PCT of 48.15.

6. Sri Lanka (6th): Sri Lanka are sixth with one win, one loss and two draws in four matches. They have 20 points and a PCT of 41.67.

7. England (7th): England are seventh after playing 13 matches. They have won four, lost eight and drawn one. England have 38 points and a PCT of 24.36.

8. Pakistan (8th): Pakistan climbed to eighth after their win over the West Indies. They have won two and lost four of their six matches. Pakistan have 16 points and a PCT of 22.22.

9. West Indies (9th): The West Indies slipped to the bottom of the table after the defeat to Pakistan. They have won two, lost eight and drawn two of their 12 matches. They have 30 points and a PCT of 20.83.

title: China's first sodium-ion electric dump truck enters service
description: Chinese companies Hina Battery and Tonly Heavy Industries say they have delivered the world's first all-electric dump truck powered by a sodium-ion battery.
fullText:
Chinese companies Hina Battery and Tonly Heavy Industries say they have delivered the world's first all-electric dump truck powered by a sodium-ion battery. The project highlights the growing adoption of this cell chemistry in commercial vehicles, even though its energy density still trails that of lithium-ion batteries.

The range of applications for sodium-ion batteries is expanding in China. Following their use in stationary energy storage systems, passenger cars and heavy-duty trucks, Hina Battery and Tonly Heavy Industries have now delivered what they describe as the world’s first battery-electric dump truck powered by a sodium-ion battery. The vehicle was handed over to mining company Sanyou Mining in July and will generate real-world operational data to support the further development of the technology.

The vehicle is based on Tonly’s TLE120 platform and is equipped with Hina Battery’s ‘Haixing’ sodium-ion battery system, which offers a storage capacity of 676 kWh. According to the manufacturer, the cells achieve an energy density of more than 165 Wh/kg. The battery can be fully charged in 20 to 25 minutes and is designed to deliver more than 8,000 charge cycles, even under regular fast-charging conditions.

The developers highlight the advantages of sodium-ion cell chemistry for mining applications in particular. Sodium-ion batteries are considered well suited to low-temperature operation and offer high cycle stability – both key requirements in mining, where vehicles often run in multi-shift operations and face extreme winter conditions. Hina Battery also says the technology enables smaller battery packs, shorter charging times and higher vehicle availability.

The latest deployment forms part of a broader trend in China. In June, FAW Jiefang announced the completion of extensive road tests of a heavy-duty electric truck equipped with a sodium-ion battery from Hina Battery. The vehicle covered more than 15,000 kilometres over almost seven months. According to FAW, the battery retained more than 90% of its usable capacity at temperatures as low as -40 degrees Celsius and is designed to achieve more than 8,000 fast-charging cycles.

Several Chinese battery manufacturers are advancing the commercialisation of sodium-ion technology in parallel. In May, CATL announced an investment of five billion yuan to expand its sodium-ion battery production capacity to 40 GWh per year. A month later, the company said it plans to equip up to 20,000 vehicles with the new battery technology this year. BYD has reported up to 10,000 charge cycles for its developmental cells, while BAIC has already presented prototypes with an energy density of over 170 Wh/kg.

However, sodium-ion technology still faces economic challenges compared to lithium-ion batteries. According to Hina Battery, sodium-ion cells currently cost between 0.5 and 0.7 yuan per Wh, compared with 0.3 to 0.5 yuan per Wh for lithium-ion cells. CEO Li Shujun expects the costs of both chemistries to converge by 2027 or 2028, with cell costs falling to around 0.3 yuan per Wh by 2028.

The technology also continues to lag behind lithium-ion batteries in terms of energy density. Last year, Tonly introduced a battery-electric dump truck with an 801 kWh LFP battery, compared with the 676 kWh sodium-ion battery used in the newly unveiled model. In addition, Tonly has already been offering a battery-swapping system for mining trucks for some time.

title: Israeli President Herzog calls antisemitism a 'contamination of societies' as hate crimes surge
description: NYPD data shows anti-Jewish incidents account for 56.9% of all hate crimes in 2026 as Israeli President Isaac Herzog warns antisemitism is a global contamination.
fullText:
Israeli President Isaac Herzog issued a stern warning about the global spread of antisemitism in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital at his Jerusalem residence.

"Antisemitism is an age-old plague which should be dealt with by everybody, by all societies. It's not an Israeli issue or only a Jewish issue," he said.

"It's a contamination of societies that starts with the Jews — never ends with them. It's the most dangerous phenomena that has to be dealt with aggressively, with no mercy, with full adjudication, and most importantly, with education," he added.

Exclusive: Israeli President Herzog Blasts Mamdani, Praises Trump, Sounds Alarm On Iran

Herzog's warning comes as newly released New York City Police Department (NYPD) data show anti-Jewish incidents accounted for 56.9% of all confirmed hate crimes since the start of 2026, even though Jewish New Yorkers make up only about 10% of the city's population.

Herzog pointed to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whom he accused of spreading hate and compromising the lives of New Yorkers.

"Mamdani does not respect my nation's right for self-determination — the Jewish people's inherent right to have a nation of their own. And he's basically spreading blasphemy, hate, antisemitic rhetoric. He should understand that he's risking his own citizens, he's risking their safety, well-being and life," Herzog told Fox News Digital.

In a video posted on social media on July 21, Mamdani called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "a war criminal" and "the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people."

Days later, Raul Morales, 51, allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" while stabbing two men on Manhattan's Upper West Side, including one who was visibly identifiable as Jewish.

Suspect Arrested After Allegedly Yelling 'Allahu Akbar,' Stabbing 2 Men In Nyc Attack

"We've seen the stabbing just a few days ago... just because somebody was dressed as an Orthodox Jew. This cannot be accepted in New York, which is a city that is dear to our heart, dear to Israelis, and dear to me personally," Herzog said.

More broadly, a report released last month by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism found that 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks across seven countries outside Israel in 2025, marking the deadliest year for such violence in the Jewish diaspora since 1994.

The J7 comprises Jewish communities in the United States, Australia, Canada, Argentina, the United Kingdom, Germany and France.

According to the report, more than 23,000 antisemitic incidents were recorded across the J7 countries last year, representing a 97% increase in violent attacks and a 136% rise in overall incidents compared with 2022.

"Of course, Israel is doing its best, but it has to be an effort with governments all over the world, law enforcement agencies, educational systems and Jewish communities, which we care about a lot," Herzog said, in reference to confronting Jew-hatred.

Referencing a recent article by professor Niall Ferguson titled "The Death of History," he said, "How much TikTok or the social networks distort the facts of history? They negate the worst and greatest horror of humankind, the Holocaust. And that's why we have to stand up together and combat it," he told Fox News Digital.

Herzog stressed that misinformation spread through distorted and superficial channels makes it easy to smear Israel on social media, but that such narratives do not reflect reality.

German Officials Warn Islamist, Far-left Rhetoric Driving Spike In Antisemitic Attacks

"[Israel] is the place where the Startup Nation flourishes. This is the place where great ideas are given to the world and contribute enormously to the world in so many great fields, from health to energy, to science, to agriculture, to food security, to what not. There's a reason why Americans who visit our country, young Americans, fall in love with this country," he said.

Growing antisemitism, coupled with polarization within and between Jewish communities and a weakening sense of Jewish identity in some places, led Herzog to launch Voice of the People in April 2023. The initiative brings together a council of 150 emerging leaders — one-third from Israel, one-third from the United States and the remainder from around the world.

Leaders are selected through an algorithm from thousands of candidates and serve rotating terms of roughly two years, developing ideas to address challenges facing the Jewish world.

The initiative held an in-person kickoff summit in March 2025 in Haifa, featuring Herzog and bringing together all council members, reflecting his belief in building the next generation of Jewish leadership, which he described as one of his main tasks.

"I'm overjoyed by the great ideas I see and feel, and I hope that around November we will have a new registration starting for the next slot, the next cohort, and I invite as many Jewish friends to register," he said.

title: 'Show me they want me' - will World Cup hero Torres stay at Barcelona?
description: Ferran Torres has come under fire from Barcelona supporters after leaving the door open to a potential move away from the club.
fullText:
Ferran Torres will return to Barcelona later this month having cemented his name in the country's football folklore following his extra-time winner to seal Spain's second World Cup triumph.

His profile and marketability has significantly grown and those around him will be keen to ensure he makes the most of a career-defining moment.

But a summer dominated by World Cup celebrations has given way to transfer speculation, fuelled by the forward's own comments during a media tour in the United States.

The 26-year-old is under contract with Barcelona until June 2027 meaning, if he does not reach an agreement with the Catalan giants, Torres will be able to negotiate with another club as a free agent from January.

So, as Barcelona's players gradually report back for pre-season, does Spain's World Cup hero's future remain at the Nou Camp?

The uncertainty surrounding Torres' future has intensified following a series of high-profile television appearances in the United States for a promotional tour with his sportswear sponsor.

Asked where he expected to be playing next season, Torres replied: "I have a contract with Barcelona but, in football, you never know.

"We are waiting to make the right decision. Right now, all I know is that I have to be in training for Barcelona on 12 August. Let's see what happens."

Asked what Barcelona need to do to keep him, he said: "Show me they want me, come to negotiate."

Reflecting on his winner against Argentina in the World Cup final, he added: "I've watched it thousands of times. When I finished the game, I didn't remember the goal. It was unbelievable. I can't describe it with words."

The speculation only increased when he was asked directly about reported interest from Paris St-Germain.

"Every time these teams want you it's a good thing," Torres said. "You never know because in football everything can change in one minute, so I have to be ready for everything."

Asked how he would approach such a career-defining decision, Torres replied: "Trying to think what is going to make me happiest."

Torres' comments have frustrated many Barcelona supporters, who believe he has been too open about the possibility of leaving the club and attempting to strengthen his negotiating position.

Fans have also taken issue with what they see as his carefully chosen wording when discussing interest from other teams, particularly given that he has never established himself as a regular starter or consistently lived up to expectations since joining Barcelona from Manchester City in 2022.

Barcelona remain relaxed about Torres' situation despite the growing uncertainty surrounding his future. They say they will speak to him when he returns to training, as planned.

He was not a regular starter under Hansi Flick last season and ended the campaign with 21 goals and three assists in 49 appearances.

But he is one of the club's most trusted and versatile attacking options, rotating primarily with Robert Lewandowski - who has since signed for Chicago Fire - as a central striker while also providing cover across the front three.

Barcelona are ultimately keen to extend his contract but any new agreement is expected to keep Torres within the existing wage structure rather than include a substantial salary increase.

Reports suggest the club would look to delay formal negotiations until September - after the transfer window has closed - so as not to affect Financial Fair Play calculations and their ability to do business during the current window.

Renewing Torres' deal would also reportedly trigger, external a payment of almost £7m to former club Manchester City, because of a clause included in his contract when he signed in the 2022 January transfer window.

Barcelona have received no formal offers for the Spain international although, as with any member of the squad, they would consider an offer if one were made.

PSG, managed by former Barcelona coach Luis Enrique, remain interested in the forward and are monitoring developments closely as Barcelona prepare to present their proposal.

The forward may feel he heads into those negotiations from a position of strength.

They come with the club still seeking a long-term number nine solution, with a move for Atletico Madrid's Julian Alvarez remaining uncertain.

That means, following Lewandowski's departure at the end of his contract in June, Torres is the only senior Barcelona forward with significant experience of playing as a central striker.

title: Soccer-FIFA apologises to members as Infantino holds crisis meeting amid stake sale fallout
description: FIFA said on Wednesday it had apologised to its member associations for mistakes made over its abandoned proposal to sell commercial rights linked to the World Cup, as
fullText:
Aug 5 (Reuters) - FIFA said on Wednesday it had apologised to its member associations for mistakes made over its abandoned proposal to sell commercial rights linked to the World Cup, as the governing body's leadership reaffirmed its support for president Gianni Infantino after a crisis meeting in Morocco.

Following the meeting in Rabat, attended by Infantino, secretary general Mattias Grafstrom and members of FIFA's management board, FIFA said its leadership had reaffirmed its full ‌support for the president while acknowledging that the handling of the withdrawn FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal should have been different.

In a statement, FIFA said a separate letter had been sent to FIFA Council members and the 211 member associations apologising ‌for the errors and promising a review.

It added that, with the proposal withdrawn, FIFA would "no longer tolerate any attacks on its integrity, good governance and due process" and would take all necessary measures to protect its reputation.

Vehicles believed to be carrying Infantino and Grafstrom were seen leaving FIFA's Africa office in Sale after the meeting, which ​came amid mounting criticism of Infantino's leadership ahead of next year's presidential election.

The meeting followed last week's withdrawal of a proposal to sell a 20% stake in a new commercial rights entity to private investors in a deal that would have raised about $4.2 billion for football development.

The proposal, which also drew scrutiny because of the involvement of a company with family links to U.S. President Donald Trump, prompted fierce criticism from European soccer's governing body UEFA and other stakeholders, who accused FIFA of poor governance and a lack of consultation.

The apology underscored FIFA's acknowledgement that mistakes had been made in the handling of his proposal for a new commercial rights body, which has become the most serious challenge to his leadership since he became FIFA president in 2016 after triggering a torrent of criticism from UEFA, several member associations and senior FIFA officials over governance ‌and consultation.

His backdown last Friday has done little to assuage those critics, most notably UEFA, ⁠which accused him of selling the soul of the game and has said it no longer has confidence in his leadership.

That has cast a shadow over Infantino's re-election for a fourth term at the FIFA Congress in Morocco in March, which had looked like a foregone conclusion two months ago.

A handful of European federations have withdrawn their backing for the Swiss Italian, but perhaps more damaging are the messages coming from ⁠Infantino's FIFA colleagues.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney also questioned Infantino's leadership on Wednesday, saying he has lost confidence in the FIFA president after learning senior advisers had not been consulted on the abandoned proposal.

"I don't have confidence in Mr. Infantino," Carney told reporters, adding that failing to inform senior executives and fellow board members of such a significant proposal "should be fatal" for any leader.

Grafstrom had sent an internal memo to staff lamenting the "sad and reproachable series of events" that led to the project being "permanently abandoned", two sources told Reuters.

"Individuals, unstable moments and unfortunate episodes come and go. The institution, its mission ​and ​its responsibility towards world football continue," the Swede added in the letter, which made no mention of Infantino by name.

His words echoed those of FIFA's Chief ​Operating Officer Kevin Lamour, who said last week that staff had been "deceived" over the plan which he ‌described as the project of one person.

Infantino's senior adviser Carlos Cordeiro resigned in protest at the plan last week. Arsene Wenger, FIFA's chief of Global Football Development, said he had not been involved in drafting the proposal, and called the decision to withdraw it "absolutely necessary".

Former Portugal great Luis Figo, who had planned to run for the FIFA presidency in 2015, said Infantino should resign over the affair, while UEFA Vice-President Laura McAllister told Reuters the controversy surrounding the abandoned proposal had brought the FIFA president's leadership to a crisis point.

Infantino has spent the past week in Morocco, which will co-host the World Cup in 2030 and whose football association has announced its continued support for him.

The meeting was widely seen as an effort to reinforce support for Infantino and ensure that he emerges from the crisis with enough backing to remain the favourite for re-election in March.

An Extraordinary Congress could be called if 43 or more FIFA member associations make a formal written request for one.

Qatar, which hosted the 2022 World Cup, Kuwait, Lebanon, Sri Lanka, Indonesia and the Philippines have declared ‌their loyalty to Infantino.

Infantino has always enjoyed a lot of support away from the traditional heartlands of the game, where impoverished football associations rely on ​FIFA's largesse to operate.

But European Leagues, which represents more than 1,300 clubs across Europe, said FIFA must not be allowed to "continue taking unilaterally disruptive decisions" that affect ​clubs, players and fans. It also criticised the "impractically short assessment timeline" of four weeks given by FIFA to study the plan ​to expand the World Cup from 48 to 64 teams for the 2030 edition.

AFRICAN ADMINISTRATORS BACK INFANTINO

Leading African football administrators have sent messages of support as Infantino looks to the continent's 54 members for backing. The ‌African confederation (CAF) has yet to take a stance.

The executive committee of the smallest and least wealthy ​regional confederation, Oceania, will meet next Wednesday to discuss their approach.

Under FIFA ​rules, the vote of San Marino, whose men's team are ranked 211th and last in the world rankings, counts as much as that of World Cup winners like Brazil, Germany, Argentina and Spain.

One clear advantage for Infantino as he looks to extend his presidency until 2031 is that no clear candidate to stand against him in March's election has yet emerged.

Jordan FA President Prince Ali bin Hussein has twice stood for the post, and he made his position clear on Tuesday when he ​accused FIFA of "blackmail", saying it had offered to help solve problems in exchange for endorsing Infantino.

"We ‌did not endorse him before and certainly will not now," Prince Ali wrote on social media.

A FIFA spokesperson rejected reports that Infantino had made promises over the host of the 2030 World Cup final.

"It is false and misleading to ​claim the FIFA president has made any promise in relation to hosting the FIFA World Cup 2030 Final. A decision will be made by FIFA in due course," the spokesperson said.

title: Players who turned World Cup heroics into big transfers
description: BBC Sport looks back at some of the players whose standout performances at the World Cup earned a big transfer.
fullText:
The World Cup is football's biggest stage, filled with goals, drama and unforgettable moments - but it can also prove to be the ultimate shop window.

World Cup heroics have transformed players' lives in the past, and Vozinha's recent move to Chilean side Colo-Colo after an impressive tournament with Cape Verde is the latest reminder that the competition still has the power to change careers.

At the age of 40, the goalkeeper's journey from the Portuguese second division to Chile's biggest club may be unique, but he is not the first to get a big move after starring on the global stage.

Here are some of the players whose standout performances at the World Cup earned them a big move.

Similar to Vozinha, Marc-Vivien Foe was an unknown name before the 1994 World Cup.

Despite Cameroon's disappointing World Cup campaign in the USA, compared to their historic run in 1990, Foe emerged as one of the team's best performers during his debut tournament.

A standout game against Brazil caught attention, which then led to a free transfer from Cameroon's Canon Yaounde to French side Lens.

Foe spent four years at Lens and helped them achieve their first league title in the 1997-98 season.

He also played for West Ham United, Manchester City and Lyon, where he won the French League Cup and Lyon's first Ligue 1 title in 2002.

Foe tragically passed away in June 2003 after he collapsed during a Confederations Cup semi-final against Colombia.

Gilberto Silva's first appearance at a World Cup came in 2002, when the tournament was hosted in South Korea and Japan.

The 25-year-old, who played in Brazil's top division for Atletico Miniero, returned home as a World Cup winner who played every minute of every game for Luiz Felipe Scolari's team.

Silva was only brought into the starting XI because Brazil captain Emerson was ruled out by injury.

But, after playing a key role in Brazil's triumph, the midfielder earned a move to Premier League champions Arsenal.

Nicknamed 'The Invisible Wall', the defensive midfielder joined the Gunners from Atletico Mineiro for about £4.5m.

During his six years in north London, Silva won two FA Cups and played a key role in the famous 2003-04 Invincibles side that went unbeaten to claim the Premier League title.

At the age of 22, Javier Mascherano announced himself on the global stage at the 2006 World Cup, where he helped Argentina reach the quarter-finals.

His performances for both his club back in Brazil and at the World Cup drew the attention of European clubs.

Mascherano initially expressed his desire to remain at Corinthians and help the club in their relegation battle.

However, he soon made the move to West Ham United in the summer of 2006 alongside his Argentina team-mate Carlos Tevez, who also impressed at the World Cup in Germany.

Mascherano had a brief spell with the Hammers until the beginning of 2007, leaving to join Liverpool where he featured in their 2007 Champions League final defeat by AC Milan.

Mascherano then played for Barcelona from 2010, winning the Champions League twice and being part of squads that won La Liga on five occasions.

At the age of just 21, Mesut Ozil emerged as one of the world's most exciting young players after he helped Germany finish third at the 2010 World Cup.

After registering four goals and four assists in seven games, Ozil was able to show off his quality and prove he was a standout performer.

Big clubs took note, and by August 2010, Ozil switched Werder Bremen for Real Madrid, for a fee of about 15m euros (£12.4m).

Copa del Rey, La Liga and Spanish Super Cup titles were to follow during his three year stay in Madrid, before becoming Arsenal's record signing for £42.4m in 2013.

James Rodriguez became one of the stars of the 2014 World Cup, scoring six goals for Colombia and winning the Golden Boot after a memorable run to the quarter-finals.

His excellent performances, including his famous volley against Uruguay, earned him a spot in Fifa's team of the tournament.

The volley against Uruguay was later voted as the best goal in the tournament by more than four million people on Fifa's website and won the Fifa Puskas Award for the best goal of the year.

Real Madrid decided to sign Rodriguez from Monaco for about 75m euros (£71m) after the tournament - a move that led to him winning multiple trophies with Los Blancos, including two Champions Leagues.

Well, you knew this one was coming.

Vozinha became a cult hero when Cape Verde claimed their first World Cup point against Spain in the group stage and his social media fame has exploded from 50,000 Instagram followers to nearly 30 million.

After helping his team reach the knockout stages, taking finalists Argentina to extra time in the last 32, Vozinha was named in Fifa's team of the tournament and even had a newly discovered species of sea slug named after him.

Vozinha's career has taken him to Slovakia, Angola, Moldova, Cyprus and, until recently, Portuguese second division side Chaves, but he has always believed himself to be a "big club player".

Joining Colo Colo, the most successful team in the Primera Division (34 titles) and Copa Chile (14), is his career "highlight".

fullText:
While some users say the wearables have changed their lives, critics voice fears over safety and privacy

With more than 7m pairs reportedly sold in 2025, Meta’s Ray-Ban smartglasses are fast becoming one of the world’s most popular gadgets.

While supporters say they are transforming photography and accessibility, critics have raised concerns about nonconsensual filming, privacy and data collection.

We spoke to users, and people who refuse to wear them, about the impact the glasses have had.

Based in The Hague in the Netherlands, Servaas wears his Meta glasses every day. He bought them for the built-in camera rather than the AI features and uses them to photograph and film walks and bike rides. “It’s an immersive experience,” he says. “I love everything tech and have done my whole life.”

He says the discreet camera means most people don’t realise he is wearing smartglasses, although he was once stopped by security at an event held in a government building because staff feared he might be recording. “For some reason, security didn’t understand. They were very scared of them [the glasses]. People said I should have expected that but I didn’t agree with them because it’s not like I’m spying.”

Despite allegations that Meta workers in Kenya viewed private footage recorded on the glasses, Servaas was not put off by the scandal. “I know Meta loves your data [but] I’m not worried about my privacy because I’ve only used them to record outside.”

For others, however, the glasses offer far more than convenience. Nikki, 59, from Devon in the UK, has been blind since birth owing to an inherited retinal disease and describes the glasses, which she received as a Christmas present in 2024, as “a real gamechanger”.

“I live in quite a rural location,” she says. “I could hear something going on ahead of me as I was walking down to the village shop. I said: ‘Hey Meta, look and tell me what’s in front of me.’ It told me there was a van unloading scaffolding. It’s things like that that I find absolutely amazing.”

While she understands concerns about privacy, Nikki worries public criticism could make the technology less accessible for people who genuinely rely on it. “What about dashcams? What about camera doorbells? What about action cameras like GoPros? People don’t complain about them,” she says. “I kind of worry that if people start going on about privacy and safety, it will be harder for those of us who genuinely benefit from the glasses.”

Yet the accessibility features have not transformed everyone’s experience. Karen Walter, 84, from San Diego, who has been living with severe hearing loss for more than 20 years, bought the glasses solely for their live-caption feature.

“Even with state-of-the-art hearing aids, I have a great deal of difficulty understanding what people are saying unless the person is very close to me and speaking directly to me,” she says. “I expected [the glasses] would be a great help in noisy environments and when I was trying to keep up with conversations involving more than two people.”

The live captions worked well during a demonstration in a quiet Best Buy store, she says, when she was “with one staffer who was directly in front of me, about two feet away”. However, she says they failed to perform in the situations for which she had bought them: “I have tried the glasses when in a group of three up to a group of seven and the caption feature just doesn’t work. There were too many people talking and too much surrounding noise.”

Not everyone is convinced the technology belongs in everyday life at all. Kiki, from the West Midlands in the UK, says she finds the idea of discreet cameras built into ordinary eyewear “pervasive”, particularly for women and children.

“If you try to take a picture with your phone, at least it’s pretty obvious,” she says. “With the glasses, you have no choice, as the camera is much harder to spot.”

Kiki says seeing people wearing the glasses in public has left her feeling uneasy.

“When someone’s just looking at you through their glasses, it worries me,” she says. “I imagine taking images secretly is far easier [than on phones]. You could just pretend to adjust your hair or cap, and press the button in a passing gesture. I’ve seen people wearing them. I saw someone wearing them in a cafe and just moved away because I felt uncomfortable.”

Although she accepts the technology could have genuine benefits, Kiki says her concern is more about the lack of safeguards. “For accessibility, absolutely,” she says. “But what bothers me is regulations often lag so far behind technology.”

“They have made me much more wary in public,” she says. “I can, however, see that people working in a shop late at night by themselves might feel safer being able to take a picture of someone harassing them.”

Pete, 44, from Northampton, believes the glasses point to a broader problem: AI-powered wearables collecting ever more personal data with too little scrutiny or regulation. “I’m not an old man shaking my fist at the clouds,” he says. “I’ve been onboard with technological advancement all my life, but with AI and Meta glasses, I’m drawing the line.”

He is more concerned about where the data ends up than covert filming. “I don’t know who’s getting the pictures at the end and what they’re doing with them,” he says. “Whether they’re not doing anything or they’re selling it to someone, and then what those people are doing with it.”

While Pete acknowledges the glasses could be transformative for blind people and other disabled users, he believes stronger safeguards are needed before they become commonplace. “I would like things like this to be of benefit to us,” he says. “I just don’t trust it.”

title: Defender Walker 'at ease' with England retirement
description: Former England defender Kyle Walker says he is "at ease" with his decision to quit international football and hoped it could lead to an extended club career, similar to that enjoyed by James Milner.
fullText:
Former England defender Kyle Walker said he was "at ease" with his decision to quit international football and hoped it could lead to an extended club career - similar to that enjoyed by former team-mate James Milner.

The Burnley right-back, who turned 36 in May, announced his retirement from the Three Lions in March after a glittering career earned him 96 caps and feature at five major tournaments.

Walker played in the final of the European Championship in 2021 and 2024 and the semi-finals of the 2018 World Cup.

England finished third in this summer's tournament in North America, although injuries to Reece James and Tino Livramento led to midfielder Declan Rice having to step in as an emergency right-back, with central defenders Ezri Konsa and Jarell Quansah also deputising.

Asked if he had retired too early from England after being left out of squads by Thomas Tuchel, Walker said "no, definitely not".

"Decisions in life you stand on what you do," he added. "I made that decision and it was a collaborative decision for me and my family. They have been through everything with me in the summers and internationals so it was not just me, myself and I making that decision.

"It was a difficult decision but one I'm more at ease with now. It was something I wanted to do and felt it was right. I spent a lot of years with England representing my country that I was very grateful for.

"The way the squad and injuries fell, maybe I might have been in with a shout but I was not to foresee that. He [Tuchel] could've always called me and I would've represented my country, but he decided not to and that's how it goes. I was not expecting a call because I was retired.

"It was Reece James, Trent Alexander-Arnold, Tino Livramento, so I was not leaving them spare, so I could enjoy some family time."

Walker was speaking at the media launch of the English Football League (EFL) season, which was staged at the National Football Museum in Manchester on Wednesday.

Burnley were relegated from the Premier League and start their Championship campaign at home on Sunday, 16 August against another side that dropped down a division in West Ham.

Walker played in 36 of the Clarets' 38 top-flight games in 2025-26 and hoped his decision not to play international football would prolong his club career.

His former team-mate Milner won 61 caps for England before retiring from international football in 2016 at the age of 30.

But the midfielder would go on to play top-flight club football for another 10 years, setting the record for the most appearances in the Premier League era, before hanging up his boots aged 40 at the end of last season after a spell at Brighton.

"I will take it season by season," added Walker, who won six Premier League titles and the Champions League at Manchester City before joining Burnley in 2025.

"I'm 36 and will be 37 at the end of the season and I will see how I feel and how my body holds up.

"I still feel good and still feel I'm playing at a good level. You look at someone like James Milner and how long he went on in his career. He retired very early [from England] and went on to achieve great things in football so hopefully I can follow in his footsteps."

title: Sprinting for GB - two years after taking up sport
description: Gloucester sprinter James Arminio is racing at the Under-20 World Championships, only two years after first stepping on to an athletics track.
fullText:
Barely two years after he first stepped on to a sprinting track, Gloucestershire teenager James Arminio will compete for Great Britain at this week's Under-20 World Championships in Oregon.

The 18-year-old, who is due to collect his A-Level results when he returns from the USA, is competing in the 100m and 4x100m relay.

"It's all happened really quickly so it's been a lot to take on whilst juggling A-Levels at the same time," Arminio told BBC Radio Gloucestershire.

"But I still have so much more to learn, I'm still new to the sport, I'm nowhere near where I need to be in terms of what I've learned. There's still much more improvement there, so much more gains to make."

It was only when Arminio, from Gloucester, started sixth form in 2024 he first got a taste of athletics, having previously played football which he says he "never took too seriously".

"My coaches always knew I was quick but it wasn't until I started track that I knew how quick I could be," he said.

Through his school he was invited to compete against other athletes from the county and eventually qualified for a regional championships.

From there, he joined Gloucester Athletics Club and linked up with his now coach Justin Smith.

Since starting consistent training, Arminio's sprint times have improved markedly and he represented Great Britain for the first time earlier this summer.

"Constantly seeing improvements, it just gives you that motivation - you're constantly seeing the times decrease, you know that if you keep doing the work that's going to keep happening," he said.

"At the start of this season, me and Justin had a chat and said the [U20] World Championships is at the end of this year, do we want to go for it? And I said 'absolutely'.

"That was the main motivation for me this season, I knew that was where I wanted to go, that was how much quicker I wanted to be."

Arminio says he is not looking too far ahead and hopes this week's competition in Eugene will be another step in his development, with his career still in its infancy.

"It would be nice to win obviously but, with the level of competition, it's going to take a lot to do well there," he added.

"I'm hoping to just get a good personal best, enjoy the experience, meet people and learn from them - take that into the future and grow from there."

title: Ryder Cup stars join Irish Open field
description: Robert MacIntyre, Patrick Reed, Francesco Molinari and Sepp Straka will play the Irish Open at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg, County Clare from 9-13 September.
fullText:
Robert MacIntyre, Patrick Reed, Francesco Molinari and Sepp Straka will play the Irish Open at the Trump International Golf Links & Hotel in Doonbeg from 9-13 September.

Defending champion Rory McIlroy and two-time major winner John Rahm are the headline attractions in a field that also contains home favourites Shane Lowry and Padraig Harrington, as well as Luke Donald, Tyrrell Hatton, and the Hojgaard brothers, Rasmus and Nicolai.

American Reed, who won the Masters in 2018, currently leads the Race to Dubai and has won twice on the DP World Tour this year.

The 36-year-old announced his departure from LIV Golf in January and is eligible to return to the PGA Tour this month.

MacIntyre, 30, has not played since finishing in a tie for 28th at the Open last month.

The Scot, ranked number 17 in the world, had said after Royal Birkdale he would be returning to the USA for the conclusion of the PGA Tour season this month before teeing it up at the PGA Championship at Wentworth and the Alfred Dunhill Links Championship.

The Irish Open takes place one week before the former of those tournaments next month.

It is expected that US President Donald Trump will attend the Irish Open as part of his visit to the Republic of Ireland.

title: Will Max Verstappen leave Red Bull? Could Fernando Alonso retire? F1’s biggest ‘silly season’ rumours
description: Four-time F1 world champion Verstappen is being heavily linked with a big-money move to Mercedes or McLaren
fullText:
Max Verstappen's future has been the topic of heated conversation for well over 18 months now, dating back to his last Formula 1 world championship triumph in 2024.

The four-time world champion, the outstanding driver of his generation, officially has a £50m-a-year contract with Red Bull until the end of the 2028 season.

However, the Dutchman is motivated by competitiveness. Red Bull have been unable to provide him with a top-tier car in the last two seasons, as illustrated by their constructors' finishing spot: third last year and, at the 2026 summer break, fourth this year. As such, Verstappen is being linked with a move away.

There is other "silly season" speculation too: Carlos Sainz is understandably disappointed with Williams' poor start to the season and is said to be looking elsewhere, while Fernando Alonso looks to be on the brink of retirement given Aston Martin's torrid plight.

Here's a round-up of the main F1 transfer stories

It is the million-dollar (or several million-dollar) question – and would have big ramifications for the rest of the grid.

Verstappen is yet to confirm his future will be at Red Bull in 2027 and, despite some post-race reactions to the contrary, the 28-year-old does look set to continue in the sport in spite of his protestations about this controversial generation of car.

The Dutchman has an exit clause in his contract allowing him to leave if he's outside the top two in the drivers' championship by the summer break – and he's currently positioned a lowly sixth in the standings, 110 points behind championship leader Kimi Antonelli.

But where would he go? Naturally, runaway leaders Mercedes seem the most obvious destination, given team principal Toto Wolff's previous flirtations with the Red Bull driver. Photos of Wolff holidaying with Verstappen and their families in Sardinia have only accentuated those rumours.

Yet Wolff has publicly stated how happy he is with his driver pairing. Antonelli, at 19, is the next big hotshot in the sport while Russell has publicly insisted he will still be with the team next year.

McLaren look to be the other viable option. Verstappen's trusted race engineer Ginapiero Lambiase joins the papaya as head of racing, perhaps as early as next year, and talks took place with the Dutchman's agent Raymond Vermeulen in June.

Yet the reigning world champions have struggled for consistency themselves this season, though they did earn a breakthrough win in Hungary through Lando Norris.

If Verstappen were to land a spot at the Woking-based squad, it seems highly likely that Oscar Piastri would be the one to make way… perhaps in a straight swap with Red Bull?

On the flip side, Verstappen has spoken in depth about his loyalty to Red Bull after more than 12 years in their programme. A year ago, he decided to stay put; he may well do the same this time around.

Alongside Aston Martin, Williams have been the big let-down of 2026.

James Vowles spoke in depth in the past few years about all his focus being on this year's car and, armed with the strongest engine (Mercedes), their chassis and reliability have been underwhelming.

After 11 rounds, Sainz has just six points to his name. And the Spaniard, who joined amid much hope of a Williams renaissance last year, is looking elsewhere.

He has been linked with a return to Alpine, having originally turned them down for Williams in the summer of 2024. Sainz drove for Renault for one solitary season in 2018.

The 31-year-old could also be a prime contender to swoop in if there's a big shift (ie Verstappen) further up the grid, whether it be a return to Red Bull (where he started his career in 2015 with sister team Toro Rosso) or otherwise.

The knock-on impact of a Sainz departure would be big, too: it could mean Franco Colapinto returns to the team from Alpine. Again, a straight swap could materialise.

This question may well be the first we get answered after the summer break.

The 45-year-old acknowledged that he will spend his three-week holiday contemplating his future in the sport, after what has been a disastrous start to the season for Aston Martin and their new engine partner Honda.

It seems very unlikely that Alonso will switch teams for 2027. The question really is: does he have faith in Adrian Newey to turn the team's form around for next year – and significantly enough that he can challenge right at the top?

The slowest team on the grid for much of the campaign so far, they have some way to go at this stage.

title: Prendergast takes four as Fire beat Super Giants
description: Ireland international Orla Prendergast takes 4-18 as Welsh Fire beat Manchester Super Giants by three wickets at Old Trafford.
fullText:
The Hundred women's competition, Old Trafford

Manchester Super Giants 85-9 (100 balls): MacDonald-Gay 18* (14); Prendergast 4-18

Welsh Fire (91 balls): Wareham 17 (12); Ecclestone 3-14

Welsh Fire won by three wickets

Ireland international Orla Prendergast took 4-18 as Welsh Fire beat Manchester Super Giants by three wickets at Old Trafford.

Playing only her second Hundred match after arriving as an injury replacement for Sophie Devine, the seamer tore through the Super Giants' top-order as the hosts slipped to 24-4.

Prendergast bowled Super Giants captain Meg Lanning for a golden duck, had Mady Villiers caught for five and then trapped Kathryn Bryce (4) lbw, before Heather Graham had Paige Scholfield (5) stumped.

India's Smriti Mandhana made 15 before she was run-out after being called through for a risky single, while Sophie Ecclestone (9) became Graham's second stumping victim.

Richa Ghosh was Prendergast's fourth wicket, caught in the covers for 11, but Ryana MacDonald-Gay top-scored from number nine, hitting an unbeaten 18 to help her side reach 85-9.

Fire reached 27 in their reply, before losing Sarah Bryce, caught and bowled by Bex Tyson for 16, while fellow opener Georgia Voll reached the same score before skying a catch off Villiers.

Ecclestone removed Freya Kemp (6) and Prendergast with successive balls, having her England team-mate clip to Lanning at short mid-on and then bowling the Ireland all-rounder. She also had Georgia Wareham caught well by Lanning for 17 in her figures of 3-14.

Graham guided Fire to a nervy victory, losing two further partners but hitting an unbeaten 16, including the winning runs as her side reached 88-7 with nine balls to spare.

The win moved Fire above Leeds Sunrisers into fourth place and two points behind Super Giants who remain third.

title: Heavyweight Parker cleared to fight after drugs ban
description: Former world heavyweight champion Joseph Parker has been cleared to fight again after his provisional suspension for testing positive for cocaine was lifted.
fullText:
Former world heavyweight champion Joseph Parker has been cleared to fight again after his provisional suspension for testing positive for cocaine was lifted.

The 34-year-old New Zealander was tested by the Voluntary Anti-Doping Association (Vada) on 25 October.

On the same day, he was beaten by Britain's Fabio Wardley at London's O2 Arena.

"I'm pleased to confirm my provisional suspension is lifted and I'll be back in the ring soon," Parker said on Wednesday.

"I've been advised to say no more for now while details are finalised. Thank you to all my supporters."

Parker has denied knowingly taking any banned substances. He had faced the possibility of a ban of up to two years, with any sanction to be determined by UK Anti-Doping (Ukad) and the British Boxing Board of Control (BBBoC).

The BBBoC confirmed to BBC Sport that Parker's provisional suspension has been lifted but said it "cannot make any further comment at this stage".

BBC Sport has also contacted Ukad, which did not oversee the original test and would need to carry out its own investigation.

Parker holds a professional record of 36 wins and four defeats. He was WBO heavyweight champion from 2016 to 2018 before losing the title to Britain's Anthony Joshua in Cardiff.

title: Key questions as Infantino faces Fifa executives
description: Fifa president Gianni Infantino will face senior leaders of football's world governing body on Wednesday. This is what is expected to happen.
fullText:
Fifa president Gianni Infantino will meet with senior leaders of football's world governing body on Wednesday as criticism of his now scrapped plan to sell off Fifa's commercial and event operations intensifies.

After secretary general Mattias Grafstrom sent a highly critical internal memo to Fifa staff, Infantino summoned members of the Fifa management board to Morocco.

Tuesday also saw chief of global football development Arsene Wenger insist he was "not involved" in Infantino's Fifa Forward Enterprise proposal, adding that aborting it was "absolutely necessary and beyond question".

Prince Ali, president of the Jordanian Football Association, then accused Fifa of creating a situation which "amounts to blackmail" over unpaid prize money and support for Infantino's re-election.

These claims have not been verified by the BBC, and Fifa made no comment when approached. But Prince Ali's statement is indicative of the strength of feeling among the member associations that oppose Infantino.

At the weekend, Uefa said it had lost confidence in Infantino's leadership. Several member associations - including Wales, with England set to follow suit - have withdrawn support for his re-election.

Now Infantino will meet with Fifa's hierarchy to try to secure his position.

BBC Sport understands the meeting will take place at Fifa's Africa office in Rabat.

It will include Grafstrom and members of the Fifa management board.

Among those in attendance will be finance chief Thomas Peyer, legal chief Emilio Garcia Silvero, chief of staff Daniel O'Toole, chief of member associations Elkhan Mammadov and media relations director Bryan Swanson.

It is unclear the intention of the meeting, but it is expected that Infantino will attempt to build bridges in an attempt to create a path to remaining as president.

However, this may not be straightforward.

In his letter to Fifa staff, Grafstrom said the events of the past week had been "a sad and reproachable series of events" which were "difficult to comprehend and accept".

On Friday, Kevin Lamour, Fifa's chief operating officer, said the private investment plan was "the project of one person". He added Fifa's own administration was "deceived".

Infantino will have to show contrition and perhaps offer a route to reform if he is to win back the support of his inner circle.

Carlos Cordeiro, Infantino's senior adviser on global strategy and governance, quit on Friday over the plan.

Cordeiro said the proposal was "a bad deal for football" and would "mortgage football's future".

Member associations had been given a deadline of 19 September to approve the plan or miss out on the extra funding that came as part of the deal.

In his resignation announcement, Cordeiro offered a series of questions which Infantino will likely face at Wednesday's meeting.

"Most troubling of all," Mr Cordeiro said, "is the absence of answers to fundamental questions.

"Why this deal? Why now? What oversight exists? Who benefits? Was there a competitive process? What governance will be in place? What will investors ultimately gain, and at what cost to football?

"These questions remain largely unanswered, and yet member associations are being asked to make a decision of enormous consequence in barely 50 days or risk being left behind.

"That is not a responsible way to determine the future of the world's game.

"This proposal has become a defining question for Fifa's future."

On top of this, Infantino may also have to map out - or could offer - a route for reform.

This may involve putting additional checks and balances in place that would make it impossible for such a plan to be devised and presented in this way again.

Perhaps he could shelve his plans for a 64-team World Cup? Or offer to open up Fifa's cash reserves?

Courting controversy and befriending Trump - the story of Fifa boss Infantino

Infantino calls executive meeting as criticism mounts

Infantino opponents threaten 'non co-operation' with Fifa

It seems unlikely that Infantino will leave his position as Fifa president by the end of Wednesday.

Infantino has, so far, shown no indication he is considering relinquishing his position. Indeed, he has been trying to rally his core supporter base around the globe.

On Tuesday we saw African countries Egypt, Morocco, Niger, Mauritania and DR Congo all issue statements in support of Infantino.

Infantino will, however, have to answer serious questions about a hugely controversial and damaging week for Fifa.

There may be those in the room who will query his ability to turn this around, especially with such fierce criticism from European countries.

Could that criticism be strong enough for Infantino to tender his resignation?

More likely, perhaps, Infantino could see this as the start of the fightback.

We may see a statement that will include an apology and a promise of change.

If Infantino does vow to fight on, Uefa and countries from other confederations must look to find other ways to oust him.

The Fifa Council could try to force Infantino's hand through an emergency meeting.

Such a gathering would be triggered if 19 of the 37 Fifa Council members call for one.

However, BBC Sport understands there are doubts that the 19 votes could be achieved.

Another step could be an extraordinary congress of the 211 Fifa member associations, which would be held if one-fifth, or 43 associations, "make such a request in writing".

So Uefa, which has 55 nations, can trigger the extraordinary congress whenever it wishes.

That would take a minimum of two months from the point it is triggered, but more likely three months, and there is no guarantee of success.

In effect, it would be a de facto election without there being another candidate as 106 votes would be needed to pass the vote of no confidence.

Infantino would have time to win back votes from those who had been angered by the investment plan.

Uefa can only really go down this route if it is confident of getting over the line.

Which leaves finding a suitable candidate to fight the election at the Fifa Congress in March.

Infantino stood unopposed when he was re-elected in 2019 and 2023 and if someone wants to battle him for the position, the deadline to announce their candidacy is 18 November.

Concacaf president Victor Montagliani is seen as the most likely unity candidate to stand against Infantino.

But there should be no expectation of success. Even at the height of the Fifa scandal in 2015, Sepp Blatter was re-elected as president eight days before he eventually resigned.

If Infantino is still in position later on Wednesday, this story could yet have a long way to run.

Inside Fifa, the expectation is that Infantino has called the meeting in Rabat in an attempt to clear the air, have a show of unity and try to achieve some alignment with his senior staff.

But while that may be the beleaguered president's intention, what remains uncertain is what kind of response he will receive from those present, especially given the highly critical statements issued in recent days by chief of global football development Wenger, secretary general Grafstrom and chief operating officer Lamour.

Some staff are asking if that could have emboldened others at the top of the organisation to speak out against him or to even insist he steps down.

It is no surprise Infantino has chosen Morocco, where he has been based over the past week.

Morocco is friendly territory for him. Not only is the country hosting the next World Cup, its national football association has come out in support of him. And it is where he still hopes to be re-elected for a fourth term at next year's Congress.

The Uefa-led rebellion against him will be hoping that it does not get that far, and that he has been forced to quit long before then.

title: Nazi warships, mammoth bones emerge as Danube River dries up
description: Water levels on the Danube River have dropped so low that dozens of World War II German battleships – and even the remains of an ancient woolly mammoth — are emerging into view.
fullText:
Water levels on the Danube River, the second longest in Europe, have dropped so low because of drought that the hulks of dozens of World War II German battleships — and even the remains of an ancient woolly mammoth — are emerging into view.

They are a curious distraction from the summer heat crisis. The Danube's record-low water levels have also forced power plants to the brink of shutting down, and governments across Central and Eastern Europe are taking steps to conserve electricity.

In the middle of the river separating Serbia and Romania, near the Serbian port of Prahovo, a rusty hull is now visible, along with a broken mast where the Nazi flag once flew.

The ships, some still laden with weapons, belonged to Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet that the Germans deliberately sank as they retreated from Romania and as Soviet forces advanced deeper into Europe near the end of the war.

At least 20 World War II wrecks of various sizes are now visible to the naked eye from the banks of Prahovo.

Ivica Gavrilovic, who has spent his whole life living beside the Danube, said the interest in the wrecks was high but access remained difficult. "People still don't know how to access the ships themselves," he said, while taking a family of three out on his small boat.

Historians say up to 200 German warships were scuttled in September 1944 near Prahovo in the Danube gorge as they came under Soviet fire. The idea behind the deliberate sinking was to slow down the Soviet advance in the Balkans. But Nazi Germany surrendered months later, in May 1945.

The sight of the old warships is a reminder that the Serbian government, with European Union financial support, has long been trying to do something about them. Some were removed from the river by Communist Yugoslav authorities, but most have remained because of the explosives they carried.

Now, however, authorities are trying to keep traffic flowing on the Danube, which flows through 10 nations, as the dropping water levels create dangerous conditions. Experts have linked the unusually hot weather to global warming and other factors.

Krsta Brandic, a Prahovo resident, said the low water levels have almost stopped ship traffic: "As you can see, the (big) ships can't pass anymore."

The old vessels have emerged before. In 2024, a trove of sunken Nazi ships, still decked out with explosives, emerged in the Danube following a blistering summer drought. Dozens of scattered ships operated by Nazi Germany's Black Sea fleet also appeared in 2022 near Prahovo after water levels reached record lows.

Meanwhile, falling water levels in the Danube unveiled bones of a mammoth in Bulgaria, a local museum director told AFP.

The bone fragments found near the northeastern city of Ruse "very likely" belonged to a woolly mammoth that lived during the Ice Age, said Nikolay Nenov, director of the Regional Historical Museum.

Specialists have so far identified a jawbone, fragments of tusks, part of a shoulder blade, and a femur with its articular head among the stash, Nenov said.

The animal is thought to have been young and the dark color of the bones may indicate that it spent a lot of time in a marshy environment, he added.

The bones are an important discovery because they are well preserved and "unlike many previous discoveries ... were concentrated in the same place," indicating that they all belonged to the same animal, Nenov said.

Woolly mammoths coexisted with early humans who hunted the cold-resistant herbivores for food and used their tusks and bones as tools.

The animals died out about 4,000 years ago. For decades, scientists have been recovering bits and pieces of mammoth tusks, bones, teeth and hair.
